Robert Robinson
RAH-bert RAH-bin-sun
proper noun
English; Robert (Germanic, “bright fame”), joined to the patronymic surname Robinson (“son of Robin,” itself a diminutive of Robert); the name of the hymnwriter who sang of grace and of the prone heart.

See also: Robert Robinson

📖 Biblical Definition

Robert Robinson (1735–1790), converted in his youth under the preaching of George Whitefield after a wayward and troubled early life, became a Baptist minister at Cambridge and a man of considerable gifts. In the flush of his early faith, at about the age of two-and-twenty, he wrote the hymn by which the whole church knows him: “Come, Thou Fount of every blessing, tune my heart to sing Thy grace.” It is a hymn of the streams of mercy, of the Ebenezer stone of help, and—most piercingly—of the honest confession of a heart still prone to wander: “Prone to wander, Lord, I feel it, prone to leave the God I love; here’s my heart, O take and seal it, seal it for Thy courts above.” Robinson knew his own frame, and in later years his own steadfastness was tried; yet the hymn stands as one of the most searching confessions of the believer’s need of sovereign, keeping grace ever penned. It teaches the church that even the saved heart must be tuned by grace, bound by grace, and sealed by grace unto the day of redemption. Robert Robinson is honored as the singer who set forth both the fountain of free grace and the sinner’s ceaseless dependence upon it.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

English hymnwriter (1735–1790), author of “Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing.”

ROBERT ROBINSON, proper noun. English Baptist minister and hymnwriter (1735–1790).

Converted in youth under George Whitefield after a wayward beginning; long a preacher at Cambridge.

Author of “Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing,” written in the early years of his faith.

The hymn confesses both the free grace of God and the heart’s proneness to wander from Him.

A gifted man whose own steadfastness was tried, yet whose hymn ministers keeping grace to millions.

📖 Key Scripture

1Sa 7:12 — "Then Samuel took a stone, and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us."

Jer 2:13 — "For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water."

Eph 4:30 — "And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption."

Php 1:6 — "Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his hymn recovers the principle of sovereign keeping grace over a wandering heart.

expand to see more

This entry is preserved to honor a hymn of rare honesty—one that names the believer’s own proneness to wander and casts him upon sovereign grace to keep him. There is no error to correct, but a searching confession to lay upon the church’s heart.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the keeping, sealing grace of God over hearts still prone to stray. “Prone to wander, Lord, I feel it, prone to leave the God I love; here’s my heart, O take and seal it”—this is no license to sin but a cry for the grace that alone preserves the saints unto glory. Let the church sing it soberly, confident that He who began the good work will perform it unto the day of Christ.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name of the singer of free grace and the heart’s need to be kept.

expand to see more

Robert — “bright fame” from the Germanic, a name of Norman kings and English commoners alike.

Robinson — “son of Robin,” a diminutive of Robert, one of the commonest English surnames.

The “Ebenezer” of 1 Samuel 7:12—“hitherto hath the LORD helped us”—stands in the second stanza.

The “fount of living waters” and the “streams of mercy” draw upon the fountain imagery of Scripture.

The sealing of the Spirit unto the day of redemption grounds the closing plea of the hymn.

Usage

"“Robinson wrote ‘Come, Thou Fount’ while yet a young man in the first fervour of grace.”"

"“We raised our Ebenezer and sang, ‘hitherto Thy help I’ve come.’”"

"“No hymn confesses the prone heart more plainly, nor pleads keeping grace more earnestly.”"
